Consult Summary:
- 19-year-old female with probable uncomplicated urinary tract infection (cystitis) presenting with dysuria, increased urinary frequency, lower abdominal ache, and pink-tinged urine today. Plan includes urine testing and empiric antibiotics.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Burning/painful urination with frequent urination and lower abdominal ache for about a week (initially described as three days; corrected to just under a week). Pink-tinged urine today; no frank blood noted previously.
- Associated symptoms: No fever, nausea, or vomiting. No back or flank pain. Bowel habit variability consistent with IBS; no new GI symptoms.
- Onset/duration: Symptoms ongoing for just under a week; initial 3-day estimate updated.
- Past medical history: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
- Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill; IBS medication starting with M (name not confirmed).
- Allergies: Clindamycin (antibiotic) allergy.
- Social history: Lives in university halls; not currently sexually active; long-term boyfriend; handles alcohol socially; tried cannabis once (recently).
- Sexual health: Last unprotected intercourse approximately 1–2 weeks ago; last menstrual period ~2 weeks ago.
- Relevant negatives: No fevers, no vomiting, no N/V, no reported back pain.

Examination:
- Not performed (no exam findings documented).

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection/cystitis.

Plan:
- Urine sample: Arrange patient to drop off a urine sample at a practice for lab testing; results to be communicated.
- Antibiotics: Offer two options—Trimethoprim or Nitrofurantoin; 3-day course; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Supportive care: Advise increased fluid intake; Paracetamol for pain as needed.
- Follow-up: If symptoms persist or worsen, return in about one week for re-evaluation.
- Red flags: Instruct to seek urgent care if fever, back pain, or vomiting develop.
- Pregnancy considerations: Acknowledged last menstrual period was two weeks ago; patient on combined OCP; no pregnancy testing data documented beyond discussion.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vitals and any physical exam findings not documented; specific antibiotic dosing (dose/route/frequency) not documented; no formal pregnancy test result.
- Internal conflicts: Onset duration described as 3 days initially, then clarified as just under a week; conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Clear overall; some hedging regarding exact onset and medication name; otherwise coherent.
